title: How to know when a sourdough starter is ready to bake with
subtitle: The float test and the three visual checks
excerpt: A sourdough starter is ready to bake with when it doubles reliably after each feeding and smells pleasantly sour. The float test offers a quick check. Consistent doubling is the more reliable guide.
sourceNotes: Float test as a readiness indicator is a standard home-baking technique. The primary assessment of starter maturity through doubling and visual activity is the approach recommended across contemporary sourdough baking literature.

glossaryTerms.definition: Dropping a small spoonful of starter into water to check whether it floats. A floating starter contains enough gas from fermentation to be active. A sinking starter is not yet ready.
The moment when the starter has risen to its maximum volume after feeding. The culture is at its most active at peak and will fall back thereafter. Baking bread at peak gives the best oven spring.

content.text: A starter that doubles within 4 to 8 hours of a feeding is ready to bake with. The three things to look for are: consistent doubling, active bubbling through the jar walls, and a smell that is sour and yeasty rather than vinegary or cheesy.
Volume. Mark the jar at feeding time with a rubber band. A starter at
has doubled and holds a slightly domed top. If it only rises 50% then falls quickly, the culture is still developing.

Bubbles. An active starter shows dense, even bubbling through the jar walls and a webby, open crumb if you scoop a spoonful. Fine bubbles concentrated at the surface only suggest the culture is not yet strong.
Smell. Pleasant sour, faintly yoghurty. A sharp, vinegary smell means the culture is hungry; a slightly cheesy or sulphurous smell means it is over-fermented. Both are signs to feed rather than bake.

, the culture is gassy and active. If it sinks immediately, it needs more time or another feeding. A starter can sometimes fail the float test but still bake well if all three visual checks are positive, the float test is a useful guide, not a hard rule.

Bake within a couple of hours of peak. A starter that has peaked and begun to fall still works, but bread made on the falling side has less spring and a denser crumb. If you miss the peak, give the starter one more feeding and wait again.
